questions.stem: Which collision rule requires a look-out by sight and hearing and by all available means?
options: Rule 5
Rule 2
Rule 9
Rule 35
questions.explanation: Rule 5 requires a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means, so electronic aids add to the look-out and do not replace it. Rule 7(a) similarly requires all available means to judge risk of collision.

questions.stem: Required navigation equipment stops working. What does NSR s. 5(3) say the master must do?
options: Log it and continue without it for the rest of the season, as normal
Replace it within seven days of the failure
Report to Transport Canada before sailing again
Restore it to effective operating condition as soon as possible
questions.explanation: Section 5(3) says the master must, as soon as possible, restore equipment that ceases to be in effective operating condition.

questions.stem: Required equipment fails in a port with no repair facilities. What does s. 5(4) require of the master?
options: Wait in port for the equipment to be delivered
Sail on the original schedule and ignore the defect until the refit
Plan a safe voyage to a port with repairs, allowing for it
Ask the crew to repair it at sea once under way
questions.explanation: Section 5(4) requires the master to plan and execute a safe voyage to a port with repair facilities, accounting for the fact that the equipment is not in effective operating condition.

questions.stem: Under s. 5(1), when may a vessel engage on a voyage without the equipment required by the NSR?
options: Whenever the voyage is in daylight
Under force majeure or to save life or property
Whenever the master signs a waiver
Whenever the voyage is under 12 hours
questions.explanation: Section 5(1) forbids beginning a voyage unless the vessel is fitted with the required equipment, except under force majeure or to save life or property.

questions.stem: Which statement best matches what the ECDIS chapter of a standard navigation text says about electronic chart monitoring?
options: Monitoring aids awareness but does not replace it; use no single aid alone
Monitoring replaces the need for a look-out when alarms are set
Alarms make human monitoring unnecessary on modern ships
Monitoring is only useful on ships over 3 000 GT
questions.explanation: The text says route monitoring does not replace situational awareness and that alarms can be missed or misread, so no single aid should be relied on completely.

questions.stem: A GNSS receiver is being spoofed. The plotter shows no alarm. How might you notice?
options: The VHF starts to produce static
The compass heading jumps by 180°
The boat symbol on the plotter turns red
The plotter disagrees with radar, bearings or depth
questions.explanation: Spoofing can offset the position slowly without an alarm. The Nautical Institute points to mismatches between the ECDIS position and radar overlay or visual bearings as a warning.

questions.stem: In a published bulk-carrier grounding, which of these was found?
options: A safety contour set to 100 m
A gyro-compass error of 30°
A shallow safety contour and a disconnected grounding alarm
A radar that had been tuned to 3 GHz
questions.explanation: The safety contour was 10 m on a ship drawing 10.63 m, and the anti-grounding audible alarm had been disconnected without anyone on board knowing.

questions.stem: In the same case, how long did the watchkeeper go without checking the ship's position after a series of course changes?
options: Less than 1 minute
More than 15 minutes
About 5 minutes
Several hours
questions.explanation: The watchkeeper did not check the ship's position or projected track for over 15 minutes after the course changes and missed the visual grounding alarm.

questions.stem: Required charts and publications must be corrected from which sources before a voyage is planned and carried out?
options: Notices to Mariners and navigational warnings
The ship's own log book and track history
The manufacturer's software updates for the plotter
The marine weather forecasts and warnings
questions.explanation: Section 146(1) requires charts, documents and publications required under the Division to be correct and up to date from Notices to Mariners or a navigational warning before being used to plan and execute a voyage.

questions.stem: What does NSR s. 144(3) require of the master during the voyage?
options: Record the position in the log every hour only
Keep the radar on the 6 nm range at all times
Send a position report to the Coast Guard at every change of watch
Show the route on a required chart and plot the position on it
questions.explanation: Section 144(3) requires the route to be displayed, and the position plotted and monitored, throughout the voyage, on a chart referred to in s. 142(1)(a). How this meets the under-100 GT exception in s. 142(3) is flagged for expert review.

questions.stem: The plotter says 0.8 nm off a headland. The radar says 0.52 nm, and the echo sounder reads 14 m where the chart shows 31 m at the plotter position. What is the best response?
options: Believe the plotter, because two instruments can be wrong together
Average the three readings and carry on
Suspect the plotter, move away from shore, and tell the master
Switch off the radar and sounder to avoid confusion
questions.explanation: Radar and the sounder fail in different ways yet both say the ship is closer to shore than the plotter does, so suspect the plotter. The gap is 0.28 nm, about 520 m. Act first, slow and alter away towards deeper water, then diagnose.
